hints: Focus on what the letters in $S_N2$ tell you, a nucleophilic substitution happening in one single concerted step.

Spot your players here: $\text{OH}^-$ from sodium hydroxide is the nucleophile, and the carbon joined to Br in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ is $\delta+$ because Br pulls electrons away.
Remember that a one-step mechanism has no time to form a separate carbocation or carbanion first, so link the nucleophile directly to that $\delta+$ carbon.
walkthrough:
**Recall what $S_N2$ really means**

Think of $S_N2$ as one smooth move. S stands for substitution, N for nucleophilic, and 2 means the rate depends on two species. There is no separate ion-forming step.

Rate rule:
$$\text{rate} = k[\text{1-bromobutane}][\text{OH}^-]$$

**Find the nucleophile and the $\delta+$ carbon**

$\text{OH}^-$ has a lone pair and a full negative charge, so it loves positive centres. It is the nucleophile.

In the C-Br bond, Br is more electronegative than C, so the bond is polarised:
$$\text{C}^{\delta+} - \text{Br}^{\delta-}$$
That carbon is electron-poor and ready to be attacked.

**Put the first step together**

Because it is $S_N2$, the $\text{OH}^-$ attacks that $\delta+$ carbon from the backside while the C-Br bond starts to break, all in one step. No carbocation is made, and no homolytic fission to radicals occurs. That direct nucleophilic attack is the first (and rate-determining) event.

options.A: Correct. In the $S_N2$ hydrolysis of 1-bromobutane, the lone pair on $\text{OH}^-$ (nucleophile) attacks the $\delta+$ carbon attached to Br. Bond making and bond breaking happen together in one step with no intermediate ion.
options.B: Incorrect. An electrophile seeks electrons, so it would never attack a carbanion in this reaction, and the nucleophile $\text{OH}^-$ is the attacker, not an electrophile. This also wrongly suggests a two-step ion-forming route.
options.C: Incorrect. This describes an $S_N1$ mechanism, where heterolytic fission of C-Br forms a carbocation first, then the nucleophile attacks. 1-bromobutane is primary and reacts with $\text{OH}^-$ by $S_N2$, so no free carbocation is formed.
options.D: Incorrect. Homolytic fission splits the electron pair evenly to give free radicals, which is for radical reactions, not nucleophilic substitution. Nucleophilic substitution uses heterolytic fission or concerted polar attack, and a nucleophile would not attack a carbocation formed this way here.
